newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-BASF predicts more record results in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BASF predicts more record results in 1997.

text.p: German chemicals giant BASF AG, fresh from reporting its second consecutive set of record results, predicted still better earnings and sales for 1997.

BASF chief executive Juergen Strube called 1996 a "peak year" and predicted 1997 would be a "special" year in which sales should reach 50 billion marks ($29.9 billion) and earnings grow at least as strongly as sales.

After a strong start to the year marked by double-digit first quarter sales growth, driven in part by higher domestic demand, Strobe, told a news conference, "We are confident that 1997 will once again be a special year for BASF."

Last year, BASF benefited from improved currency market relationships and expanding operations to post a 5.5 percent rise in sales to 48.7 billion marks. Pre-tax profits climbed 6.9 percent to 4.4 billion marks while earnings per share, calculated according to the DVS method, jumped 16.7 percent to 4.40 marks.
BASF said that special charges for restructuring and other factors, reduced by extraordinary income from insurance claims, totalled 517 million marks.

Unlike German competitors Hoechst ERG and Bayer ERG, BASF fared relatively well in the fourth quarter, posting a 13.9 percent rise in sales to 12.6 billion marks and a 1.3 percent rise in pre-tax profits to 1.05 billion marks.
Mirroring record results, BASF raised its 1996 dividend to 1.70 marks from 1.40 marks, and Strobe, well-known for downplaying predictions, again promised his shareholders more joy this year.
The stock market, relishing the upbeat outlook, pushed BASF shares up 0.65 marks to 61.65 marks.

BASF chief financial officer Max. Detroit Key also said there was still more room for the shares to climb, particularly in view of the group's plans to establish a "competitive edge" and willingness to let dividend payoffs reflect earnings.
Like last year, BASF expects its health and nutrition business, particularly pharmaceuticals, as well as its oil and gas business to be engines for growth.
Sales in health and nutrition jumped 14.1 percent to 9.1 billion marks while sales in the oil and gas sector soared 23.8 percent to 5.2 billion marks last year.

The group's largest business segment, plastics in fibres, posted a three percent drop in 1997 sales to 12 billion marks with colorants and finishing products, the second largest area, climbing 4.8 percent to 11.28 billion marks. Chemical sales, suffering from price pressures, rose only 0.6 percent to 7.3 billion marks.

Asked about possible future take-over plans, Strobe said the group's war chest was filled again, only two years after its high profile purchase of the drugs division from Britain's Boots, but cautioned this should not be taken to mean a target was in sight or that BASF was in talks with anyone.
"I was specifically vague about this topic and cannot add anything more specific," he said.
Again unlike its German competitors, BASF also said that it was sticking to its strategy to build up its generic drugs business, of products whose patent protection has expired.
"We realise other groups are retreating in this area, but herein we see a certain opportunity," Strobe said, adding BASF would consider making new acquisitions in this area at the right price.

BASF also said it would maintain its 5.2 percent stake in US generics giant VAX Corp. and was not worried about the impact of possible sales of VAX units. There has been talk that VAX would be forced to sell some of its units after plans to merge with US drugs wholesaler Bergen-Brunswig collapsed.
BASF plans to raise its fixed asset investments to 3.8 billion marks from 3.6 billion marks in 1996, with 1.4 billion marks earmarked for Europe, the group's biggest market.
One billion marks would also be invested in North America, where BASF posted a 6.5 percent rise in sales last year.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.670 German Marks)
